title: Rate down, pressure down
objective: Recognize atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response, weigh rate control, rhythm control and anticoagulation, and monitor for hypotension during IV rate control

brief.situation: 15:30 on a progressive care unit. Mr. Castellano, 66, is two days after a hip replacement. Telemetry shows a new irregular, narrow rhythm at 150. He feels his heart 'fluttering'.
handover: Echo last year: ejection fraction 55%. Blood pressure 118/74 a moment ago, SpO2 95%.

The provider has ordered the IV rate-control infusion with blood pressure every 5 minutes during it, to stop the infusion and call for a systolic below 90 or any dizziness, and is deciding about anticoagulation with the surgeons.
The rapid response team and the provider are reachable at once.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Assess and act as you think the patient needs. Each assessment takes the time on its button.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: Mr. Castellano's rate is falling, but so is his pressure, and he is dizzy. What is happening, and what do you do?

parts.label: What is happening
parts.criteria: IV rate control for new AF has caused hypotension with symptoms; that is the danger to watch for; unstable AF with hypotension may need cardioversion, and anticoagulation must be weighed against surgical bleeding.
parts.modelAnswer: The rate-control drug is dropping his pressure: systolic under 90 and dizzy. That's the complication we were watching for. If he's unstable from the AF itself, cardioversion becomes the question, with anticoagulation weighed against his surgery.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Stop the infusion now; call the provider and rapid response; lay him flat; keep monitoring; hand off.
parts.modelAnswer: Stop the infusion, lay him flat, call the provider and the rapid response team now, and hand off the times.

unsafe.headline: A fast extra push
unsafe.body: IV rate control is titrated by order and watched for hypotension; it is never pushed faster to chase a number.

worsened.headline: Shock on the infusion
worsened.body: Cycle the pressure during IV rate control and stop at the threshold the order sets.

wrongRoute.headline: Left running
wrongRoute.body: A falling rate doesn't make a falling pressure acceptable. Stop and call.

target.headline: Stopped in time
target.body: Pressure cycled, ECG read, and the infusion stopped within minutes of hypotension. That is the expert path.

recovered.headline: Recovered, with delays
recovered.body: Check how long the hypotension went before the infusion stopped.

time_up.headline: Unresolved
time_up.body: New AF with a falling pressure needs a decision within minutes.

scoring.modelReasoning: New AF at 150 after surgery with a normal ejection fraction: the ordered IV rate control is appropriate, with the pressure cycling every 5 minutes. The danger is hypotension. When the systolic falls under 90 and he is dizzy, the infusion stops at once and the provider and rapid response team come; cardioversion and anticoagulation, weighed against his surgical bleeding, are the provider's next decisions.

efQ.ask: While you assess: in which patient should a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker be avoided for rate control?

choices.label: Ejection fraction under 40% or decompensated heart failure

efQ.explain: Patients with EF < 40% or hypotension should be managed with amiodarone or digoxin; avoid calcium channel blockers in acute decompensated heart failure.

unstQ.ask: While the team takes over: AF that itself causes hypotension is treated how?
unstQ.explain: AF causing hypotension is unstable and should undergo synchronized cardioversion, with anticoagulation considered.
